identity.title: POCUS 2-point/3-point compression ultrasound of femoral and popliteal veins

technique.how: High-frequency linear probe, patient supine with hip externally rotated. Image the common femoral vein at the saphenofemoral junction (and femoral vein at the adductor canal for 3-point), then the popliteal vein with the knee flexed; at each site apply firm transverse compression every 1-2 cm until the vein walls coapt fully. Non-compressibility or visible echogenic thrombus is positive.
technique.prerequisites: Trained operator; ultrasound with linear probe; patient able to expose the groin and popliteal fossa.
technique.contraindications: Avoid compressing over open wounds, recent groin catheter sites, or a visibly free-floating thrombus.

interpretation.positive_finding: A non-compressible proximal vein has pooled specificity ~97-98% for DVT (LR+ roughly 30), sufficient to start anticoagulation in most patients pending formal duplex.
interpretation.negative_finding: Full compressibility at all points has pooled sensitivity ~90-96% (false-negative rate ~4%); with a low/moderate pretest probability plus negative D-dimer this excludes proximal DVT, otherwise repeat imaging in 5-7 days or formal whole-leg duplex.
interpretation.pitfalls: Isolated femoral-vein (adductor canal) and calf DVT are missed by 2-point protocols; lymph nodes, Baker cysts, and superficial thrombophlebitis mimic thrombus; inadequate compression in obese or edematous legs and chronic residual thrombus cause errors.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: anticoagulate and confirm; negative with low/moderate probability and negative D-dimer: stop; negative with high probability: formal duplex or repeat POCUS in 5-7 days.

estimates.target_condition: Lower-limb DVT (emergency physician-performed compression ultrasound, any protocol)
estimates.population: ED patients with suspected DVT; 16 studies, 2379 patients; operators emergency physicians with variable training
estimates.reference_standard: Radiology/vascular-laboratory colour-flow duplex ultrasound or angiography
estimates.quote: weighted mean sensitivity of EPPU compared to the reference imaging test was 96.1% (95%CI 90.6-98.5%), and with a weighted mean specificity of 96.8% (95%CI:94.6-98.1%)

estimates.target_condition: Lower-limb DVT (2-point POCUS: common femoral + popliteal)
estimates.population: ED patients with suspected DVT; 9 studies, 1337 patients; emergency physicians (attending or resident)
estimates.quote: 2-point POCUS had similar pooled sensitivity [0.91; 95% confidence interval (95% CI), 0.68-0.98; P = .86) and specificity (0.98; 95% CI, 0.96-0.99; P = .60)

estimates.target_condition: Lower-limb DVT (3-point POCUS: common femoral, femoral, popliteal)
estimates.population: ED patients with suspected DVT; 8 studies, 1035 patients; emergency physicians
estimates.quote: as 3-point POCUS (sensitivity, 0.90; 95% CI, 0.83-0.95 and specificity, 0.95; 95% CI, 0.83-0.99). The false-negative rates of 2-point (4.0%) and 3-point POCUS (4.1%)

estimates.target_condition: Lower-limb DVT (2-point POCUS protocol, updated pooled estimate)
estimates.population: ED patients with suspected DVT; 26 studies pooled through February 2023; emergency physician operators
estimates.reference_standard: Reference standard imaging (radiology duplex/whole-leg ultrasound or venography)
estimates.quote: pooled sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and NPV for the 2-point POCUS protocol were 92.32% (95% CI: 87.58-97.06), 96.86% (95% CI: 95.09-98.64)

sources.citation: Pomero F, Dentali F, Borretta V, et al. Accuracy of emergency physician-performed ultrasonography in the diagnosis of deep-vein thrombosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Thromb Haemost. 2013;109(1):137-145.

Lee JH, Lee SH, Yun SJ. Comparison of 2-point and 3-point point-of-care ultrasound techniques for deep vein thrombosis at the emergency department: a meta-analysis. Medicine (Baltimore). 2019;98(22):e15791.

Zaki HA, Albaroudi B, Shaban EE, et al. Deep venous thrombosis (DVT) diagnostics: gleaning insights from point-of-care ultrasound (PoCUS) techniques in emergencies: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Ultrasound J. 2024;16(1):37.
Wells PS, Owen C, Doucette S, Fergusson D, Tran H. Does this patient have deep vein thrombosis? JAMA. 2006;295(2):199-207.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use a single negative POCUS to exclude DVT in high pretest probability or when symptoms are confined to the calf; do not use to exclude PE (a negative leg scan does not lower PE probability meaningfully).
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Phlegmasia, suspected iliac/IVC thrombosis, or hemodynamic instability suggesting PE require formal imaging and urgent management regardless of POCUS result.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Meta-regression shows higher accuracy when the initial scan is by an attending emergency physician with dedicated DVT POCUS training rather than a resident (Lee 2019); false-negative rate ~4% in both protocols.
safety_scope.skill_assumption: Emergency physician or hospitalist with focused compression-ultrasound training (published cohorts used brief dedicated courses plus supervised scans); accuracy assumes ability to obtain full venous coaptation at each landmark.

extraction_notes: All estimates come from meta-analysis abstracts (Pomero 2013 not open access; Lee 2019 is PMC6709014 but abstract numbers were sufficient). LRs are not reported in abstracts and were not computed to avoid pooling on non-bivariate inputs. Pomero pools mixed 2-/3-point protocols; Lee 2019 separates protocols and is preferred for protocol-specific counselling; Zaki 2024 (26 studies) gives an updated 2-point estimate (3-point: sensitivity 89.15%, specificity 92.71%). Wells 2006 RCE cited as index for pretest-probability stratification.
